source: DHS OIG covert test via ABC News (2015) TSA Red Team
finding: DHS covert testers got mock explosives or banned weapons past TSA checkpoints in 67 of 70 tests. Report not public; figures come from briefed officials.
numbers: 67/70 failed (about 96%); press rounded to 95%. Dozens of busy airports, unnamed. In one test a magnetometer alarm fired but a fake bomb taped to the back was missed in the pat-down. TSA had spent $540M on screening equipment and $11M on training since 2009 without noticeable gain.
limits: Secondhand report of an unpublished audit. No per-airport data, no protocol, no confidence interval. Testers are skilled, not random smugglers, so it is an upper bound on real-world miss rate.
agent_relevance: A red team shows the whole system fails but not which fix works. Treat a high break rate as a cue to inspect the process.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Red team
finding: Defines the roles. Pen test is announced; red team adds physical entry and surprise with no warning to the blue team. White team sets rules of engagement. Purple team is a temporary red plus blue mix giving fast feedback.
numbers: FAA red teams test about 100 US airports a year; began after Pan Am 103 (1988), paused after 2001, resumed 2003 under TSA. Army red team office created 2004; Marine red team billets staffed June 2013; three red teams reviewed the bin Laden intelligence (2011). Physical ops: at least three operators, several days of recon.
limits: Tertiary source. Role definitions are convention, not tested constructs; no study compares team structures.
agent_relevance: Map to our schema: red = adversarial critic operator, white = program code that sets rules and counts, blue = repair step. Purple (fast feedback loop) is the useful part.

source: Deng et al. (2024) PentestGPT: Evaluating and Harnessing LLMs for Automated Penetration Testing
finding: Raw GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Bard do well on single sub-tasks but lose context over a whole test. A three-module scaffold (reasoning, generation, parsing, with a task tree) raised sub-task completion.
numbers: Sub-task completion: GPT-3.5 42 (23.07%), GPT-4 95 (52.20%), Bard 50 (27.47%) of 182 sub-tasks. PentestGPT gains 228.6% over GPT-3.5 and 58.6% over GPT-4. Failure causes counted: session context lost 74, deadlock operations 45, false source-code reading 37.
limits: Small benchmark (10 targets, 182 sub-tasks), human runs the commands, 2023 models. Later papers show it collapses on harder targets.
agent_relevance: Context loss is the main failure of one long chain. Supports an external state record (task tree) held by code.

source: Isozaki et al. (2025) Towards Automated Penetration Testing: Introducing LLM Benchmark, Analysis, and Improvements
finding: Builds an automated end-to-end pentest benchmark with machines graded easy, medium, hard. Compares GPT-4o and Llama 3.1-405B inside the PentestGPT tool.
numbers: On easy machines Llama 3.1-405B beats GPT-4o in every category; gap narrows on medium; on hard both struggle (DevGuru lowest). Llama beat GPT-4o on 7 machines, tied on 4.
limits: Few machines, one run each, quantised open model; no confidence intervals. Model ranking is not stable across difficulty.
agent_relevance: Ranking flips with difficulty, so a one-number benchmark misleads. Tune the scaffold on hard cases.

source: Happe and Cito (2025) On the Surprising Efficacy of LLMs for Penetration-Testing
finding: Review of LLM pentesting to mid-2025. Argues it works because pentesting is pattern matching under uncertainty. Lists reliability, reproducibility, safety, cost and accountability as open blocks.
numbers: Context: ISC2 estimates a 4.7 million shortfall of security staff (gap up 19.1% in 2025). Reasoning models struggle with function calling. Fixes split into single-agent (self-challenge, state management) and multi-agent (combining outputs).
limits: Narrative review, no pooled effect size. Authors build in this field.
agent_relevance: Run-to-run reliability is the real gap, not peak score. Report variance.

source: Lin et al. (2026) Comparing AI Agents to Cybersecurity Professionals in Real-World Penetration Testing (ARTEMIS)
finding: First live-network comparison: 10 professional pentesters versus 6 existing agents and the new ARTEMIS scaffold on a university network of about 8,000 hosts in 12 subnets.
numbers: ARTEMIS placed 2nd overall: 9 valid vulnerabilities, 82% valid-submission rate, better than 9 of 10 humans. Humans found 3 to 13 valid findings each, 49 unique total. Cost: A1 $291.47 ($18.21/h), A2 $944.07 ($59/h), humans about $60/h. Claude Code and MAPTA refused the task; Incalmo stalled in recon (0 findings).
limits: One network, one engagement, n=10 humans, time capped. Agent has more false positives and cannot use GUIs (80% of humans found an RCE on a Windows box via a GUI console that ARTEMIS missed).
agent_relevance: Agents are strong at breadth and parallel enumeration, weak on false positives and tools they cannot see. Verify findings with code or a separate checker.

source: Lin et al. (2026) ARTEMIS hint-level test and human strategy analysis
finding: When asked to find vulnerabilities humans had found, ARTEMIS did well only with detailed hints. With informational or host-only hints it moved on to other low-severity findings.
numbers: Five hint levels (high, medium, low, informational only, host only), two hours each. Human active typing time did not correlate with success. Weaker humans leaned on scan output; the top two balanced scanning with manual validation.
limits: One agent configuration, few target vulnerabilities, not repeated across seeds.
agent_relevance: The agent satisfices on easy findings and leaves the hard one. A forced step that names the neglected branch could help.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Cybench: A Framework for Evaluating Cybersecurity Capabilities and Risks of Language Models
finding: 40 professional CTF tasks from 4 competitions, difficulty set by human first-solve time (2 minutes to 24 h 54 min, 747x range). Eight models tested.
numbers: Unguided success: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 17.5%, GPT-4o 15.0%, others 10 to 20%. Subtask-guided up to 27.5%. Non-zero success on 73% of tasks with first-solve time up to 11 minutes; none solved above 11 minutes. Hardest task took humans 24 h 54 min (136x the 11-min limit).
limits: CTF tasks have a single path; 2024 models. Scores have risen since.
agent_relevance: Human first-solve time predicts agent difficulty. Intermediate checkpoints (subtasks) help.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Cybench scaffold comparison
finding: For GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, four scaffolds (structured bash, action-only, pseudoterminal, web search) were compared. Model choice and subtask guidance moved results more than scaffold format.
numbers: Unguided 17.5% versus subtask-guided up to 27.5% for top models. One task of 40 is 2.5 points.
limits: Only two models in the scaffold comparison; small task count.
agent_relevance: Giving intermediate checkpoints beat changing the prompt format. Decompose into verifiable subgoals.

source: Nakano et al. (2025) Guided Reasoning in LLM-Driven Penetration Testing Using Structured Attack Trees
finding: A deterministic task tree built from MITRE ATT&CK constrained the LLM so it could not wander into unused libraries or repeat tactics.
numbers: 10 HackTheBox exercises, 103 subtasks. Guided pipeline completed 71.8% (Llama-3-8B), 72.8% (Gemini-1.5), 78.6% (GPT-4). Self-guided baseline: 13.5%, 16.5%, 75.7%, using 86.2%, 118.7%, 205.9% more queries.
limits: Small benchmark. Gain is huge for weak models and small for GPT-4 (78.6 vs 75.7). Baseline is one tool.
agent_relevance: Code-enforced structure helps weak models most and saves queries. Supports program-owned transitions.

source: Shen et al. (2025) PentestAgent: LLM Agents for Automated Penetration Testing
finding: Multi-agent system with retrieval over pentest knowledge for recon, vulnerability analysis and exploitation. Claims better completion and efficiency on its own benchmark.
numbers: Abstract gives no headline number. Later third-party reruns (PentestGPT V2, PentestEval, PEP paper) find it drops sharply on harder targets.
limits: I read the opening pages only; comparisons come from other papers. Own-benchmark results favour authors.
agent_relevance: Self-reported wins shrank in independent reruns.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Automated Penetration Testing with LLM Agents and Classical Planning (CHECKMATE)
finding: Out-of-the-box Claude Code with Sonnet 4.5 beat all earlier research pentest systems. Faults: loses the plan, weak complex reasoning, poor use of specialised tools. A classical planner on top (CHECKMATE) fixed part of this.
numbers: CHECKMATE beat Claude Code by over 20% on benchmark success; time cut 54% (7.75 min average on 20 shared tasks); cost cut over 50%. Stability: coefficient of variation of cost 0.129 and time 0.093 in the 100% success group versus 0.451 and 0.325 in the 75% group. Example: 3 steps versus 26 for Claude Code, which repeated and quit early.
limits: Vulhub known-CVE benchmark; three repeats per task. Authors built the competitor setup.
agent_relevance: A plain coding agent beat the pentest-specific research stack. Add a planner on top and measure run-to-run stability.

source: Yang et al. (2026) PentestEval: Benchmarking LLM-based Penetration Testing with Modular and Stage-Level Design
finding: 346 tasks across six pentest stages in 12 scenarios; nine LLMs plus three agent systems. Weak at attack decision-making and exploit generation.
numbers: End-to-end pipelines succeed 31%. Attack Decision-Making and Exploit Generation average about 0.25. Best models 0.34 and 0.32 (DeepSeek-R1) versus GPT-3.5-Turbo 0.07 on attack prioritisation; CVSS static baseline 0.245. Ground-truth intermediate outputs raise success from 0.31 to 0.50, then 0.53. Three expert annotators, Krippendorff alpha used.
limits: Scored against expert answers, so valid alternate attack paths may count as wrong.
agent_relevance: Errors compound across stages; fixing one early stage buys 19 to 22 points. Check each stage before passing on.

source: Deng et al. (2026) What Makes a Good LLM Agent for Real-world Penetration Testing? (PentestGPT V2)
finding: Analyses 28 systems and reruns 5 on three benchmarks. Splits failures into Type A (missing tools, fixable by engineering) and Type B (planning and state, persist across models). Root of B: no real-time estimate of task difficulty.
numbers: V2: 91% peak (89% mean) on XBOW 104 web tasks with Claude Opus 4.5 versus best baseline 61% (49% relative); roots 12 of 13 PentestGPT-benchmark machines; 4 of 5 hosts on GOAD versus at most 2 for prior systems. Baselines on XBOW range 27 to 49% across models. Tool layer dominates short tasks; difficulty-aware search and memory give gains on multi-step ones.
limits: Authors' own system and table. GOAD is 5 hosts and omits social engineering and time pressure (authors say so).
agent_relevance: Difficulty estimation and branch pruning cut over-commitment to dead ends. Matches a code-side budget per branch.

source: Singer et al. (2025) Incalmo: An Autonomous LLM-assisted System for Red Teaming Multi-Host Networks
finding: Frontier models with existing tools (PentestGPT, CyberSecEval3, CAI) can't run multi-host red team exercises. A two-layer design (LLM plans high-level tasks, expert task agents execute) fixes most of it.
numbers: MHBench: 40 emulated networks of 22 to 50 hosts. Incalmo reached critical assets in 37 of 40; best prior systems 3 of 40. Successful runs took 12 to 54 minutes and about $15 in LLM credits.
limits: Emulated networks built by authors; no active defender. In the ARTEMIS live test Incalmo's rigid task graph stalled at recon (0 findings).
agent_relevance: Big gain from putting the abstraction layer in code, but a rigid graph can fail in the wild.

source: Xie et al. (2026) LLM-Based Penetration Testing in the Presence of Honeypots
finding: Treats deception as a budget problem: an LLM attacker must engage or drop a host when it looks fake. A detector-guided policy raised confirmed real hosts.
numbers: At the $5 budget the full policy confirmed 3.66 real hosts versus 3.00 fixed-budget and 2.33 random (about +22% and +57%). Without the pre-connect detector: 3.66 to 3.33 hosts, wasted honeypot cost 0.18 to 0.61, entry rate 58% to 63%. No stopping rule: honeypot cost 0.500; rule-based 0.438. At $2 no clear advantage (1.33 vs 1.00).
limits: Tiny samples (averages over three), controlled testbed, defender does not adapt. Gain appears only at larger budgets.
agent_relevance: Blue-side deception is the counter; an agent that cannot drop a bad branch wastes budget. Stopping rules need evidence.

source: Muzsai et al. (2024) HackSynth: LLM Agent and Evaluation Framework for Autonomous Penetration Testing
finding: Planner plus summariser agent tested on 200 CTF challenges (PicoCTF and OverTheWire) across several models; sweeps temperature, top-p and token budget.
numbers: GPT-4o was best, better than its system card suggested. Per-model percentages not extracted by me.
limits: Abstract-level reading only; files were lost before I could extract tables.
agent_relevance: Sampling temperature and token budget matter; report them.

source: Lin et al. (2026) ARTEMIS scaffold effect on Cybench
finding: ARTEMIS scored higher than baseline GPT-5 on Cybench, but the authors say this is sampling variance, not real uplift. On the live network it clearly beat Codex and CyAgent.
numbers: Scaffold benefit shows on long open-ended tasks, not short CTF ones. A1 reached similar vulnerability counts to A2 at about a quarter of the cost.
limits: Authors state the Cybench difference is within noise.
agent_relevance: Do not claim scaffold lift from a short benchmark.

source: Cross-paper comparison: independent reruns versus own-benchmark claims
finding: Systems reported on their own benchmarks (PentestAgent, VulnBot, AutoPT) score only 27 to 49% on XBOW in a third-party rerun, and fall behind plain Claude Code with Sonnet 4.5 in a second rerun (2512.11143).
numbers: XBOW baseline range 27 to 49%; PentestEval end-to-end 31%; in ARTEMIS Claude Code and MAPTA refused, Incalmo 0 findings.
limits: My own comparison across papers with different models and tasks; not a controlled meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Independent reruns shrink claimed gains. Rerun our own results on held-out items.

source: Search note: no controlled trial of red-team effect on defence found
finding: In the sources read I found no randomised study of red team versus no red team on later defender outcomes, and no replication of the TSA figure. Human evidence is the ARTEMIS cohort (n=10) and press reports.
numbers: Zero controlled trials found; one live human cohort n=10; one audit figure 67/70.
limits: Absence in a limited search (APIs partly rate-limited), not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: The belief that red teaming improves defence is untested by randomised data. Use it as a heuristic and test inside our own loop.

source: GAO covert testing of airport screening (2007-2008) [not opened]
finding: Recalled, not verified: GAO covert tests in 2007-2008 reported investigators passing liquid explosive component and improvised device parts through checkpoints at several airports.
numbers: Number of airports not verified.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite numbers until checked.
agent_relevance: Suggests the TSA 67/70 pattern is not a one-off.

source: DHS OIG follow-up covert tests (2017) reported failure rate [not opened]
finding: Recalled, not verified: a later DHS IG round was reported in press to show a similar or worse failure rate, which would be a repeat of 2015.
numbers: Press-reported rate around 80%, not verified.
limits: Not opened. Lead only.
agent_relevance: If it holds, finding failures did not lead to a fix in two years.

source: Schneier (2008-2016) security theater critique of airport screening [not opened]
finding: Security commentary argues checkpoint screening is largely show and covert tests reveal it. Opinion, not data.
numbers: None.
limits: Not opened. Opinion.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Singer et al. (2025) Incalmo failure analysis of existing systems
finding: With GPT-4o, Sonnet 4 and Gemini 2.5 Pro existing offence systems succeed on only 3 of 40 multi-host environments. Authors blame the interface: low-level commands overload the model.
numbers: 3 of 40 environments for prior systems versus 37 of 40; networks of 22 to 50 hosts.
limits: Authors define benchmark and system. No human red team baseline.
agent_relevance: Abstraction level changes success more than model choice. Cut what the model must handle per step.

source: Deng et al. (2026) PentestGPT V2 transient versus persistent failure
finding: Some failures shrink as models improve (context capacity, instruction following, tool use, domain knowledge). Others persist: planning, state management, knowing which branch is worth pursuing.
numbers: Four difficulty dimensions: horizon estimation, evidence confidence, context load, historical success.
limits: Failure typing done by authors from traces; no inter-rater figure extracted.
agent_relevance: Where scaling won't help, the scaffold should: branch scoring, stop rules, code-held state.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Claude Code ablation in the PEP study
finding: Ablation swapped the agent shell (Claude Code to OpenInterpreter) keeping Sonnet 4.5, and swapped the model keeping the shell. Human-in-loop PentestGPT fell sharply after the first milestone.
numbers: Compared PentestGPT, CAI, Gemini Code Assist, PentestAgent, Codex (o4-mini or Gemini 2.5 Pro) and Claude Code+Sonnet 4.5; Claude Code best on almost all milestones.
limits: Exact ablation numbers not extracted; qualitative.
agent_relevance: Both model and agent shell matter; iterative command debugging is a large share.
